output.headline: Andy Burnham's Labour draws progressive voters back as tactical voting reshapes the race, poll finds
output.standfirst:
Andy Burnham is drawing progressive voters back to Labour to stop Nigel Farage, a poll of more than 8,000 people finds, with tactical voting potentially pushing Reform UK into fourth place

• How Labour’s majority depends on five progressive voter types – in charts

  • UK politics live – latest updates
output.bodyHtml:
Labour could come within touching distance of a majority at the next election, a major poll has found, if tactical voting proves as widespread as progressive voters suggest – a shift that would also push Reform UK into fourth place.

Andy Burnham is drawing a significant number of left-leaning voters back to Labour, the results suggest, motivated by a wish to stop Nigel Farage.

The poll of more than 8,000 voters, shared with the Guardian, shows the prime minister’s most successful electoral strategy would be to unite the centre and left bloc of voters while the right remains split, and suggests a widespread openness to voting tactically.

The approach marks a shift from the tactics of Keir Starmer’s Labour before the 2024 general election, when the party sought to attract more conservative older voters instead. Some in Labour may be unsettled by the parallel, since the same strategy was used for Ed Miliband’s failed bid in 2015, albeit before Reform’s arrival as a major electoral force.

Related: From idealists to struggling sceptics: how Labour’s majority depends on five progressive voter types – in charts

Conducted on the eve of Labour’s annual conference in Liverpool, the poll shows a significant shift of left-leaning voters towards Burnham’s Labour, encouraging those in the party weighing an early election while Reform’s ratings ebb and leftwing parties such as the Greens appear to be losing momentum.

Since April, twice as many voters have returned to Labour from the left as from the right.

Survation and the progressive activist site 38 Degrees carried out the previously unreleased research, including a seat-by-seat MRP model, during Burnham’s first month as prime minister.

Labour would be the largest party in parliament if an election took place today, the poll suggests, winning 272 seats – a four-point lead worth 42% of parliamentary seats from 28% of the vote.

Reform would become the official opposition on 153 seats, representing 24% of seats – the same as its vote share – while the Conservatives would fall to third place with 85.

A far higher share of voters in the tightest marginals say they are open to voting tactically when asked to name their preferred party – a sign of how fluid the polls remain. Two hundred seats are decided by under five points in total, meaning a two- to three-point swing could move about 100 seats likely to decide a future election.

Labour and the Conservatives would benefit if voters switch to one of the two frontrunners in their seats rather than their preferred party – a shift that would cut Reform UK’s seat count dramatically.

About 18% of voters in seats where tactical voting would make a substantial difference say they are willing to switch but have not yet done so; if they did, Reform UK would be reduced to 62 seats and Labour would rise to 319 – six short of a majority.

Of the 91 seats where Reform would cease to be the most likely winner, 46 would go to the Conservatives and 43 to Labour, though the projection is unlikely to be exact at this stage in the electoral cycle.

In 59 seats – among them the Wrekin, Torridge and Tavistock, and North West Cambridgeshire – Reform’s chances of winning fell by more than 50 points; all three have Reform as the most likely leader under the “normal” assumptions but lose out to the Conservatives once more tactical voting is factored in.

The base modelling of the MRP gives Reform a 51% chance of winning a tight race in Rawmarsh and Conisbrough, but that falls sharply once tactical voting increases, with a 76% chance of Labour holding the seat instead. In 2024, the now-chancellor, John Healey, held the seat with 49% of the vote, with Reform in second place on 28.6%.

In Bassetlaw, tactical voting would lift Labour’s vote share from 32% to 40%, enough that the forecast winner shifts from Reform, with a 77% chance, to Labour, with a 58% chance – even though Reform’s own vote share also rises, from 35% to 40%. The Conservatives, Liberal Democrats and Greens would lose supporters if this switching took place.

Newark, held by the Conservative-turned-Reform MP Robert Jenrick, is forecast to flip to the Conservatives under both scenarios; heavier tactical voting would lift the chance of a Conservative win from 68% to more than 99% should Labour backers vote Conservative to stop him.

Damian Lyons Lowe, Survation’s chief executive, said: “Estimating tactical voting is a complex consideration, but the mechanics here are simple. Four in 10 voters are currently backing a party that can’t finish in the top two where they live and are willing to vote tactically.

“But when we ask whether they would lend their vote to the stronger local contender in a two-horse race, around half said yes. That gap – worth some 18 points of the national electorate – is an enormous untapped reservoir for parties looking to squeeze voters.

“Should these voters act as they say, our model shows Reform falling from second place to fourth, losing around 90 seats, despite its own vote share actually going up. Reform-leaning Conservatives will consolidate too. Reform doesn’t collapse; it risks being outnumbered, seat by seat, by voters coordinating around whoever is best placed locally on the left and right.”

Progressive voters living in seats such as Labour-held Southend would be unlikely to switch to the Conservatives even if they were technically best placed to beat Reform at the next election, which shows the limits of predictions around tactical voting – a limitation sharpened by the sheer number of seats Labour won in 2024 from the Conservatives where the party has been polling as low as third over the past year.

Labour is also gaining considerable numbers of voters back from other leftwing parties, though not from Reform, the poll suggests. The share of Labour’s lost 2024 voters going to the Greens, Liberal Democrats, Plaid Cymru or the Scottish National party has fallen from 60% to 46%; on the right, the share lost to Reform or the Tories has fallen from 27% to 24%.

Veronica Hawking, the campaigns director at 38 Degrees, said the polling pointed to a far more optimistic public mood than before the Labour conference last year, alongside significant expectation that Burnham needed to deliver.

“There are signs of optimism and even hope, but what has not changed is the way voters are crying out for bold action, fast,” she said. “The results show a huge amount of common ground between voters, especially when it comes to the cost of living. Voters who have moved in different directions since the general election two years ago are united by the fact that action on the cost of living crisis will have the single biggest bearing on their future vote.”
